name: Dahlak Archipelago
blurb: Mangroves, seagrass and reefs of the Red Sea, with dugongs and turtles.

tip.title: Remove the tiger sharks
tip.text: Tiger sharks eat sea turtles and dugongs. Set Tiger shark to -100% and watch the turtles and dugong rise, then the seagrass they graze and the sponges hawksbills eat.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong tropical light reaches the shallow reef flats and seagrass beds, powering algae, seagrass and the symbiotic algae inside corals.

nodes.name: Warm, salty Red Sea water
nodes.desc: The enclosed Red Sea is warm and salty, and its clear water carries drifting plankton across the shallow shelf around the islands.

nodes.name: Muddy tidal flats
nodes.desc: Sheltered, muddy intertidal shores and salt flats where mangroves root, and where dead plant matter is broken down.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, mangrove leaves, plankton and carcasses, returning nutrients to the water and sediment.

nodes.name: Reef algae
nodes.desc: Turf and macroalgae growing on reef rock and shoals, grazed by fish such as parrotfish and by green turtles.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting microscopic algae that feed zooplankton and filter feeders such as sponges. General ecological knowledge.

nodes.name: Seagrass
nodes.desc: Fast-growing seagrass of shallow sandy bottoms; Halophila is a favoured food of dugongs.

nodes.name: Grey mangrove
nodes.desc: One of the few mangroves of arid Red Sea shores; its aerial roots trap sediment and it excretes salt through its leaves.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting animals, many of them copepods, that graze phytoplankton and feed corals and small reef fish.

nodes.name: Reef sponges
nodes.desc: Filter feeders on reef rock and caves that strain plankton from the water and are the main food of hawksbill turtles.

nodes.name: Reef-building corals
nodes.desc: Corals build the fringing reefs and shoals around the islands, catching zooplankton and relying on symbiotic algae for extra energy.

nodes.name: Parrotfish
nodes.desc: Reef fish that scrape algae from rock and coral with beak-like teeth. Their role here is general reef ecology.

nodes.name: Green turtle
nodes.desc: Mostly grazes seagrass and algae as an adult; juveniles are more carnivorous. Tiger sharks are its main predator.

nodes.name: Dugong
nodes.desc: Grazes seagrass, favouring Halophila and Halodule, and its feeding reshapes the beds; the Red Sea holds important populations.

nodes.name: Hawksbill turtle
nodes.desc: Feeds mainly on selected sponges, which ties it closely to coral reefs; sharks are among its few predators.

nodes.name: Reef planktivores
nodes.desc: Small schooling reef fish that pick zooplankton from the water above the coral. Their role here is general reef ecology.

nodes.name: Groupers
nodes.desc: Ambush predators of reef fish and crustaceans, hiding among coral heads and ledges. General reef ecology.

nodes.name: Lesser crested tern
nodes.desc: Plunge-dives for fish in salt water and breeds in island colonies; the archipelago is an Important Bird Area.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A wide-ranging top predator that eats sea turtles, dugongs, seabirds, fish and dolphins, and also scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: Spinner dolphin
nodes.desc: Recorded in the Dahlak area; a small, fast dolphin that hunts schooling fish. Tiger sharks can prey on dolphins.
